title: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
subtitle: Positive test, pain, collapse: theatre

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage: diagnosis and initial management (NG126)

sources.org: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG) and Association of Early Pregnancy Units
sources.title: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy (Green-top Guideline No. 21)

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Blood transfusion (NG24)

red_flags.text: Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain and collapse, syncope or shock: ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise.
Shoulder-tip pain, pain on defaecation, or peritonism in early pregnancy: haemoperitoneum.
A positive pregnancy test with no intrauterine pregnancy seen and free fluid in the pelvis or Morison pouch.
Relative bradycardia can occur with haemoperitoneum. A normal heart rate does not exclude major bleeding.
Atypical presentations: diarrhoea, dizziness and vague pain. Ectopic pregnancy is a recognised cause of maternal death when it is dismissed as gastroenteritis.

do_now.text: Urine or serum pregnancy test in every woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain or collapse.
Shocked woman with a positive test: two large-bore cannulae, crossmatch, activate the major haemorrhage protocol, and call the gynaecologist and anaesthetist to go to theatre.
Do not delay theatre for a formal ultrasound in a haemodynamically unstable woman with a positive test and suspected rupture.
Transfuse red cells and components according to the major haemorrhage protocol; avoid large crystalloid volumes in active bleeding.

assess.text: Last menstrual period, contraception (an intrauterine device or progestogen-only method does not exclude ectopic), previous ectopic, tubal surgery, pelvic infection, assisted conception.
Haemodynamic status trended over time, abdominal and gentle pelvic examination.
Rhesus status: every woman having surgical management needs it known.

investigate.text: Transvaginal ultrasound in the stable woman: an adnexal mass separate from the ovary, with or without free fluid, and an empty uterus.
Serum hCG, full blood count, group and crossmatch, coagulation.
Bedside abdominal ultrasound for free fluid in the unstable patient, without it delaying theatre.
Pregnancy of unknown location in a stable woman: serial hCG at 48 hours and specialist early pregnancy unit follow-up.

resuscitate.text: Restore circulation with blood; permissive approach to blood pressure until bleeding is controlled in theatre.
Anti-D immunoglobulin for rhesus-negative women having surgical removal of an ectopic pregnancy, per NICE NG126.

definitive.text: Surgery for ruptured ectopic, significant pain, an adnexal mass of 35 mm or more, a visible fetal heartbeat, or an hCG of 5000 IU/L or more, per NICE NG126.
Laparoscopy is preferred to laparotomy when the surgeon is experienced; laparotomy is appropriate in the shocked woman when it is the fastest route to control.

Salpingectomy when the contralateral tube is healthy. Consider salpingotomy when there are risk factors for infertility such as contralateral tubal damage, with follow-up hCG because of the risk of persistent trophoblast.
Medical management with methotrexate is for the stable woman with an unruptured ectopic who meets the NG126 criteria. It is never an option for rupture.

escalate.text: Senior gynaecologist and anaesthetist for every unstable woman, at the same time as theatre is called.
General surgeon on call who finds a haemoperitoneum in early pregnancy: control bleeding and call gynaecology; do not leave the woman bleeding while waiting.
Interstitial, cervical, caesarean scar and abdominal pregnancies need specialist management and may need interventional radiology.

notes: Every woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain gets a pregnancy test. Not doing one is the error, not the result.
The shocked woman with a positive test is a theatre case. Her ultrasound is done by the surgeon through the laparoscope.
After surgery, ask about the experience. Pregnancy loss is a bereavement, and clinicians often forget to acknowledge it.
